blocks.p: The Armv7 Laboratory runs programs in the 32-bit ARM instruction set (A32) in your browser, one instruction at a time, or one clock cycle at a time on a single-cycle, a multicycle and a pipelined processor, each drawn as it works. Its processors follow the microarchitecture of Sarah L. Harris and David Money Harris's textbook Digital Design and Computer Architecture: ARM Edition; the meaning of every instruction follows ARM's architecture reference manual.

The textbook's processor runs a small set of instructions: ADD, SUB, AND and ORR with a register or an immediate, LDR and STR with a positive offset, and B, each with a condition. The Instructions view runs a larger subset, and the processor views' Extended datapath adds the instructions of the textbook's Chapter 7 exercises on a design of this application's own.

refs: Digital Design and Computer Architecture: ARM Edition
S. L. Harris, D. M. Harris. Morgan Kaufmann (Elsevier), 2016. ISBN 978-0-12-800056-4. Chapter 6: architecture; Chapter 7: microarchitecture.

blocks.p: Nothing is installed and nothing is uploaded: the laboratory runs entirely in your browser.

ol: Type a program in the editor, or open one from Templates.
Assemble it (Ctrl+Enter). Errors are listed in the console with their line.
Step (F10) or run (F5). Step back (Shift+F10) undoes a step.
Choose the Single-cycle, Multicycle or Pipelined view to watch a processor run the same program, one clock cycle per step.

blocks.p: The processors run only the textbook's instructions unless you choose "Extended datapath" in the instruction-set menu. The template "Base instructions only: the sum 1 to 10" runs on the base design.

dl: One instruction per step: the editor, the listing with each instruction's word in hexadecimal and binary and its fields, the registers and the CPSR flags N, Z, C and V, the call stack, the counters, the memory and the console. An instruction whose condition fails is shown as skipped.

The processor of the textbook's Chapter 7, drawn in this application's own layout. Each step is one clock cycle and one instruction: the connections the instruction uses are highlighted, the multiplexer inputs it selects are marked, and the control signals show their values. Class path shows all the connections of one instruction class.
A tab of the Single-cycle view: the cycle in register-transfer notation, each line followed by the same line with this cycle's values, and a table of every signal.
A tab of the Single-cycle view: the Main Decoder and ALU Decoder tables with the rows in use, and the PC Logic and Conditional Logic with this cycle's values.

A tab of the Single-cycle view: the critical path of the present instruction and of each instruction class, and the clock period they set, from illustrative delays you can edit. Critical path draws the present instruction's path with its arrival times. In the Multicycle view: the critical path of the present cycle and of each state, the clock period the slowest state sets, and the time of the run so far compared with the single-cycle processor's, from the same delays. In the Pipelined view: the critical path into each clocked element, stage by stage, with the register file's half-cycle paths counted twice; the clock period they set; and the program run on all three processors, with the time each takes.
A tab of the Single-cycle, Multicycle and Pipelined views: chosen signals over the cycles run so far; select a cycle to go to it.

The multicycle processor of the textbook's Chapter 7, drawn in this application's own layout. Each step is one clock cycle, one state of the controller: the connections the state uses are highlighted and the state is named on the control unit. Instruction ▶ runs the rest of the instruction, up to the next Fetch; ◀ Instruction steps back to its Fetch. State diagram shows the controller's ten states in place of the datapath, with the present state filled, the transition into it drawn heavy and the next one dashed. Extended datapath, in the instruction-set menu, shows this application's own extension of the processor.

A tab of the Multicycle view: the outputs of every state with the present state's column marked, the next state, the Instr Decoder and ALU Decoder, and the PC Logic and Conditional Logic with this cycle's values.

A tab of the Multicycle view: IR, Data, A, WriteData, ALUOut and the delayed CondEx, what each holds now, whether the next clock edge writes it and with what, and why the processor needs it; then what the edge writes to the PC, the registers, the memory and the flags.
A tab of the Multicycle view: one row per instruction, one column per clock cycle, each cell naming the state; select a cell to go to that cycle.

The pipelined processor of the textbook's Chapter 7, with its complete hazard unit, drawn in this application's own layout. Each step is one clock cycle, in which five instructions can each be in a stage: the strip above the drawing names them, and the drawing highlights the connections each one uses. A register that keeps its contents at the next clock edge is marked stall, one that is cleared flush. Hazard handling switches parts of the hazard unit off, to show what goes wrong without them; Stop on stops a run at a stall, a flush or a taken branch.

A tab of the Pipelined view: one row per instruction, one column per clock cycle, each cell naming the stage; ‖ marks a cycle held in a stage, ✕ an instruction removed, ○ a bubble. Select a cell to go to that cycle. Repeated loop iterations can be folded.

A tab of the Pipelined view: what each of the five stages does in this cycle, in register-transfer notation and then with this cycle's values: the fetch and the next PC, the register reads, the ALU's operands and where they are forwarded from, the condition check, the memory access and the write-back; a stall, a flush or a bubble is said in words.
A tab of the Pipelined view: this cycle's forwarding, stalls and flushes in words, and the hazard unit's equations with their values.
A tab of the Pipelined view: the cycles lost so far, by cause and by instruction, and the cycles per instruction built as the textbook's Example 7.7 builds them.
A tab of the Pipelined view: what each pipeline register holds, and whether the next clock edge holds or clears it.
A tab of the Pipelined view: every signal of the cycle, by stage.

blocks.p: Every instruction is conditional. The Condition Check compares the instruction's Cond field with the flags and gives CondEx; four AND gates let the decoder's requests PCS, RegW, MemW and FlagW through only when CondEx is 1. An instruction whose condition fails therefore still passes through the datapath, but writes nothing: no register, no memory, no flags and no PC other than PC + 4.

R15 is the PC. When an instruction reads R15 it gets the address of the instruction plus 8 (PCPlus8, from the second +4 adder); a write to R15 goes to the PC. A branch adds its offset to that value in the ALU.

Signal names are the textbook's: RegSrc, ImmSrc, ALUSrc, MemtoReg, ALUControl, FlagW, CondEx, PCSrc and the others. The RISC-V laboratory names similar signals differently, after its own textbook; the meaning, not the name, carries over. The textbook writes PC′ for the next PC; the drawing uses PCNext, the name in the textbook's hardware description.

The Extended datapath is this application's own design, not the textbook's: it adds a shifter before the ALU (the textbook's Example 7.3), NoWrite for the compare and test instructions (Example 7.2), a four-bit ALU control with the flags as an input for ADC, SBC and the shifter's carry, an A3 multiplexer and a link input for BL, a byte unit for LDRB, and subtraction of the offset for negative offsets. It runs CMP, CMN, TST, TEQ, MOV, LSL, LSR, ASR, ROR and shifted register operands, ADC, SBC, RSB, EOR, BIC, BL, LDRB and negative LDR and STR offsets. Immediates must have rotation 0 in both processors.

The processors stop with an error instead of doing what the hardware would do with an instruction it cannot execute correctly: an instruction outside the processor's set, an unaligned word access, or a write of an odd address to the PC.

The multicycle processor breaks each instruction into steps of one clock cycle and reuses its parts between them: one memory for instructions and data, and one ALU, which also adds 4 to the PC. Five registers that the program cannot see hold what one step passes to the next: IR the instruction, Data a word read from memory, A and WriteData the registers read, and ALUOut the ALU's result.

A finite-state machine of ten states, S0 Fetch to S9 Branch, drives the datapath; its outputs depend on the state alone. Every instruction starts with Fetch, which reads it into IR and adds 4 to the PC, and Decode, which reads the registers and computes the PC plus 4 again: the instruction's address plus 8, the value it reads for R15. In all, B takes 3 cycles, a data-processing instruction and STR 4, and LDR 5 (the textbook's Example 7.5).

The condition is checked in every state, but CondEx reaches the gates of PCWrite, RegWrite and MemWrite one clock edge late, through a register, so that flags written by an instruction in its ExecuteR or ExecuteI state cannot stop its own write-back. An instruction whose condition fails still passes through all of its states; only its writes are suppressed.
Where the textbook leaves a select as don't-care, the processor drives 0. In MemAdr this makes the R15 input read ALUOut, the instruction's address plus 8, so STR R15 stores that value.

When a condition fails, the gates it holds at 0 are marked in both processor views, with CondEx = 0 in the single-cycle drawing and CondExDelayed = 0 in the multicycle one, and the write paths are drawn muted.

With the same illustrative delays, Decode is the slowest state: a branch reads R15 through the ALU and the Result multiplexer before the register file. The multicycle clock is therefore about half the single-cycle one, but each instruction takes three to five cycles; the Timing tab compares the two on the program you run.

The Extended datapath of the multicycle processor is this application's own design, not the textbook's. It carries the single-cycle Extended datapath's parts across: a shifter between WriteData and the SrcB multiplexer, a four-bit ALU control with the flags as an input, and NoWrite, which here comes from the Instr Decoder because the ALU Decoder sees ALUOp = 00 in ALUWB. A Byte unit before the Data register loads the byte of LDRB in MemRead. BL takes two added states: Link writes the PC, the address plus 4, to R14 and puts the target in ALUOut, and BranchL writes the PC from ALUOut. The target cannot wait for the Branch state, because register A reloads at every clock edge and in Link R15 reads the PC.

The pipelined processor divides the single-cycle datapath into five stages, separated by registers: IF fetches the instruction, ID decodes it and reads the registers, EX computes, MEM reads or writes the data memory, and WB writes the result back. The textbook names them Fetch, Decode, Execute, Memory and Writeback and adds a letter, F, D, E, M or W, to each signal's name: InstrD is the instruction in the Decode stage. A new instruction can start in every cycle, so once the pipeline is full one instruction completes per cycle.

The control signals are decoded in ID and travel with their instruction through the pipeline registers. The condition is checked in EX, where the flags are kept: CondExE lets PCSrc, RegWrite and MemWrite through to the later stages only when the condition holds. Because the flags are both written and tested in EX, an instruction that sets them and a conditional instruction right behind it need nothing more. The register file is written in the first half of a cycle and read in the second, and R15 reads as PCPlus8D, which is PCPlus4F of the instruction being fetched.

When an instruction needs a result that is not yet in the register file, the hazard unit forwards it to EX from the MEM stage (ALUOutM) or the WB stage (ResultW), the newer one first. A load's data arrives only at the end of MEM, so an instruction that uses it right away waits one cycle in ID while a bubble, an instruction that does nothing, goes into EX. A taken branch is decided in EX: the two instructions fetched after it are removed. A write to R15 holds the fetch until it reaches WB. In the textbook's Example 7.7 these cost 2 cycles for a dependent load and 3 for a taken branch, against 1 for any other instruction.

The hazard unit compares the register fields of the instruction in ID with the load in EX whether or not that instruction reads them, and an STR in EX looks like a load to it, because the decoder gives STR MemtoReg = 1 where the textbook leaves a don't-care. Such a stall gains nothing; the view names it a stall no register needs. These are the textbook's design, kept as it is.

One equation is changed. As the textbook gives it, StallF holds the PC whenever a write to R15 is in ID, EX or MEM, even when a taken branch in EX is loading its target: a branch followed straight away by a write to R15, such as BEQ followed by MOV PC, LR, would lose the target and run on in the wrong place. Here StallF is released while a taken branch is in EX (StallF = (LDRstall OR PCWrPendingF) AND NOT BranchTakenE); the view names the cycles where this matters. The textbook leaves the pipelined processor's HDL to an exercise, so no hardware description was compared with this behaviour.

Hazard handling Forwarding only and None take parts of the hazard unit away. Without stalls and flushes, a load's result can be used too early and the instructions after a taken branch or a write to R15 run as well; without forwarding, the results of the last two instructions are not seen. The registers then end with values the program did not intend, which the Hazards and Lost cycles tabs explain.

The Extended datapath of the pipelined processor is this application's own design, not the textbook's; it places the single-cycle Extended datapath's parts in the stages. BL needs its own address plus 4 in R14, so PCPlus4F is kept in the Fetch/Decode register and carried with the instruction to Writeback, and an A3 multiplexer in Decode writes R14 instead of Rd. The shifter sits in Execute, between the second forwarding multiplexer and the SrcB multiplexer, so a forwarded value is shifted too; the ALU and the shifter read the C and V flags in Execute, where the instruction ahead has just written them, so ADC and SBC need no stall. NoWrite travels to Execute and holds the RegWrite gate at 0 for TST, TEQ, CMP and CMN. In Writeback a Byte unit takes the byte LDRB loads, and the result multiplexer has four inputs. The hazard unit treats LDR and LDRB as loads, by ResultSrcE, so an STR no longer causes a stall no register needs. BL's link value needs no forwarding: BL is taken, so the instruction at its target reads R14 in Decode while BL writes it in Writeback.

ul: One instruction per line, with an optional label (loop:) and a comment after ; or //.
A condition or S follows the mnemonic: ADDEQ, SUBS, BNE.
Immediates start with #: #10, #0x3F, #-4 in an offset.
Memory operands: [Rn, #offset]. The Instructions view also accepts indexing, register offsets, LDM, STM, PUSH and POP.
A branch to itself, B ., ends the program.
The code starts at address 0; .data starts at 0x10000; SP starts at 0x100000.

blocks.p: File ▸ Exercise… lists practice exercises written for this application, in three groups: the base processor's instructions, which also run in all three processor views; the Chapter 7 extensions, for the Extended datapath; and instruction-level forms, for the Instructions view. Each opens with a starter program. Its tests write data into memory, run your program on the instruction-level model until B ., and compare the registers and memory it leaves with the expected values. No solutions are included.

dl: Step / step back (in a processor view, one clock cycle)
Leave the editor (Tab inside it indents)
Resize panes (Shift for larger steps; Enter restores)

blocks.p: The laboratory sends nothing anywhere. Your programs and settings are kept in this browser only.
